newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian data underpins hopes of modest recovery.
newsitem.headline: Australian data underpins hopes of modest recovery.

text.p: Australia's prospects for improved growth through 1997 were enhanced on Friday when February retail trade data showed that consumers appeared to have returned to the stores following a disappointing Christmas.
But while improving, there was no danger that the economy was accelerating at such a speed as to require the brakes to be applied in the form of a rate rise yet, economists said.
Retail trade rose 0.8 percent in Feburary, official figures showed. It was seen as a strong figure because it followed a very large 2.7 percent rise in January retail trade.

"Today's result represents the second consecutive month of strong retail sales, suggesting that consumers have now returned to the shopping malls they deserted in the second half of 1996," Nomura Research senior economist Andrew Pease said.
Economists said the data fitted in with anecdotal evidence that spending had picked up from early in 1997, and which had remained strong into March and April.
"Consumer spending has been the missing link in the economic recovery," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said. "It looks like it's coming back strongly."
The February rise took retail trade to 4.4 percent above its trough of last September. Over the past year, retail trade was up 3.3 percent, its highest annual increase since last August.
"Numbers like this indicate that we've passed a turning point in the economy and an acceleration is underway," SBC Warburg senior economist Guy Bruten said.

The strong start to the year in retail trade follows trade data on Thursday showing that exports have also been strong in the first two months of year, and economists said both should make solid contributions to first quarter growth.
However, the data on the day was not all one-sided. The retail trade data showed some patchiness across sectors, and seperate figures showed the building approvals fell 3.7 percent in February.

A small fall had been expected after the very strong 10.4 percent rise in January but not only was the fall larger than expected, the composition of the fall suggested more weakness than economists had been factoring in.
The January rise was dominated by rises in multi-dwelling approvals, which had been expected to unwind while approvals for private houses were expected to strengthen.
Instead, private houses were down 5.6 percent while other dwelling units fell 1.6 percent in February.
"There is a housing recovery out there,it just isn't very robust yet," Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton said.
The net result, economists said, was that while growth would lift through 1997, it would not be at a rapid pace. Accordingly, there was no need for monetary policy to be adjusted.

"Economic conditions are improving but are still a long way short of justifying anything other than a 'leave rates on hold' stance from the Reserve Bank," Westpac economist Stephen McNabb said. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
